summary: This RFC notes that TCP and UDP sit far apart in the kinds of service they offer, and examines transaction processing, where short request and response exchanges are common. It looks at what a better-suited transport service would need to offer.

eli5.summary: A phone call is overkill for a quick question, while a postcard may get lost. This asks if there is a better way in the middle.

questions: why is tcp not ideal for transaction processing
what is a transaction transport protocol
tcp vs udp for request reply
what is a conversation in transport protocols
subtitle: A 1985 call for a transport protocol that sits between TCP and UDP for request and reply traffic.

tldr.problem: TCP and UDP sit far apart. TCP costs too much setup for a quick request and reply, while UDP is unreliable and limited to a single small packet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists what transaction applications need and sketches the attributes of a new protocol: reliable delivery, no explicit connection setup or teardown, a two-packet exchange in simple cases, minimal idle state and message fragmentation.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion document, not a standard and not a concrete protocol proposal. It was written to spur work in the Internet research community.

sections.title: The Gap Between TCP and UDP
sections.content:
The DoD Internet protocol suite offers two transport protocols: TCP for virtual circuits and UDP for datagrams. The memo argues these are points in the space of possible transport service attributes that are quite "far apart".

It focuses on transaction processing applications, whose needs fall into the gap between the two. The goal is to characterize a possible new transport-level protocol for them. The status note is clear that the memo does not represent a standard, nor even a concrete protocol proposal.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to send messages: a careful phone call (TCP) and a quick postcard (UDP). Some jobs need something in the middle.

sections.title: What Transaction Traffic Looks Like
sections.content:
The memo lists the typical traits of transaction processing communication:

  • Unsymmetrical: a client always starts a transaction, and a server answers. Often this is one request and one reply, but it can be a longer dialog.
  • Simplex transfers: data never needs to flow in both directions at once.
  • Short duration: typically hundreds of milliseconds up to tens of seconds, never hours.
  • Low delay and few data packets: the data often fits in one or a few IP packets.
  • Message orientation: the natural unit is a whole message (a record), not a stream of bytes.
sections.eli5: A transaction is like asking a shop clerk a quick question: you ask, they answer, and you are done in a moment.

sections.title: Example: Name Servers
sections.content:
Name servers (RFC 882, RFC 883) show the dilemma. TCP is fine for bulk updates of a name server's database, but costs a lot in circuit setup and teardown for single queries. UDP avoids that cost but has two serious problems: packets may be lost, duplicated or reordered, and a query or response is limited to the 548-byte maximum of a single UDP packet.

Name servers were then using UDP, and their requests are idempotent, so lost or repeated queries do no harm. Still, the memo expects UDP to become unusable for more queries as replies grow and as flakier paths come into use. A resolver cannot tell packet loss from server queueing delay, so implementations chose long fixed timeouts (e.g., 30 seconds or more). The memo also argues that applications should not have to implement their own retransmissions or know numbers like 576 or 548.

It suggests a new protocol with at-least-once reliable delivery, no explicit connection setup or teardown, fragmentation and reassembly of messages, and minimal idle state in client and server.
sections.eli5: Looking up a name should be quick. A postcard might get lost and make you wait ages, and a phone call takes too long to set up for one question.

sections.title: Example: Distributed Operating Systems
sections.content:
Distributed operating systems such as Cronus, Locus and the V-System use private protocols tuned for local networks, relying on the inherent reliability of a LAN and simple single-packet exchanges. Efforts were under way to extend them across the Internet. A suitable standard transaction transport could simplify future distributed systems.

The essential need is packet economy: the same minimal two-packet exchange used on the LAN should work across the Internet. That implies no explicit connection setup or teardown, and implicit ("piggy-backed") acknowledgments, so the reply acts as the acknowledgment of the request and a new request acknowledges the previous reply. These systems also want at-most-once, ordered delivery (relaxed for idempotent requests) and a clean fit with the proposed Internet multicast facility using host groups.
sections.eli5: If a reply can also count as saying "got it", you only need two messages instead of many.

sections.title: Objectives for a New Protocol
sections.content:
The memo lists attributes of the proposed protocol:

  • Reliable delivery: exactly once, or the sender is told. It must handle loss, duplication and reordering, and old duplicate requests must not cause erroneous actions. Applications may ask for relaxed reliability for idempotent requests or notifications without reply.
  • Minimum packets: a simple two-packet exchange in the simplest case.
  • No explicit connection setup or teardown, but some implicit "soft" state between two addressable entities, called a conversation.
  • Minimal idle state: only enough to recognize old duplicates and suppress unneeded ACKs.
  • Fragmentation and reassembly so applications need not know packet size limits.
  • Message orientation and multicast capability.

Open issues it names are the choice of addressable entity, timeout dynamics (Internet delays range over four decimal orders of magnitude, yet short exchanges leave little chance to measure them), flow control for multi-packet messages without a circuit setup, and implementation efficiency. The memo says further study is needed.
sections.eli5: The wish list: a quick two-message chat that never loses a message, never does the same thing twice, and does not keep a lot of notes when nobody is talking.

sections.title: Scope, RPC and Conclusion
sections.content:
The memo expects RPC (Remote Procedure Call) and message-passing facilities to be built on top of the proposed transport layer. They would handle further issues that are not part of the communication substrate: the application interface (binding and stub generators), structured data encoding, server location and binding, and authentication and access control.

It concludes that transaction-based communication will be increasingly important on the Internet and that there is a pressing need for an appropriate transport protocol. The work grew out of discussions in the New End-to-End Protocols taskforce.
sections.eli5: The new protocol would just carry messages. Fancier tools for calling remote programs would be built on top of it.
